prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms, bringing frequency standards to the 1e-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep B005 as a single-part prize for Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye, and the first-round exchange has sharpened rather than changed my reasons. The achievement is one idea, trapping many atoms at a magic wavelength so that the light shift cancels for the clock transition, followed by a realization that took fractional uncertainty to about 1e-18 and that has been reproduced and surpassed with strontium, ytterbium and other species in several countries. That makes the physics settled and not interpretive. Two names map onto two distinct steps, the concept and first lattice spectroscopy on one side and record accuracy, systematic control and many-body effects on the other, and the three-seat limit is not strained. The chair's question about an explicit criterion between B005 and B014 deserves a direct answer. My criterion is whether the central claim of the work is established beyond the open questions of interpretation, and whether the credited names can be defended against the strongest omitted claimants. B005 passes both tests more cleanly, while B014 passes the first only for the existence of the phases and not for their origin, and meets the second only with a contested trio. The pending redefinition of the second is an application, not a condition for the validity of the invention. I am also not persuaded that a third prize in precision measurement is redundant: the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems enabled this work, but many-atom interrogation in a magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct step with a distinct statistical and systematic budget.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains subject proximity to the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and a committee that reads precision metrology as one programme could call a third award incremental. A second is credit. Other lattice-clock groups in Paris, at PTB and elsewhere, ion-clock groups reaching comparable accuracy by another route, and ultrastable-laser developers are outside the two names, and my recollection of early priority between the Tokyo and Boulder efforts is from memory and has not been checked against the record. If that record showed that Ye's contribution is better described as realization at record accuracy than as co-invention, the citation wording matters, and I have tried to meet this by citing invention and realization jointly while keeping the claim tied to the magic-wavelength lattice and not to timekeeping in general. Finally, if the committee decides that a new phenomenon outweighs a measurement advance, B014 is the stronger case, and I would then want the credit settled carefully.

responses.point: Mehlig moved from KPZ to B014, argues that the prediction-then-confirmation structure is decisive, and asks whether a clock is a new discovery about nature or an instrument achievement.
responses.response: That is the sharpest framing of the question in the room and I want to answer it directly. A lattice clock does not discover a new phase of matter, but the invention changes what can be observed: it lets many atoms be interrogated without first-order light shift or Doppler and recoil broadening, so relativistic redshifts across centimetres and bounds on drifting constants become measurements. I count that as discovery-grade enabling work in the same sense as earlier measurement prizes, not as a lesser category. I accept your point that the pairing mechanism in twisted bilayer graphene does not affect the existence of the correlated states, and I have moved a little toward B014 on that. We still differ on the credit. Your own list shows the trio is a compromise, with Bistritzer treated first as junior and later accepted, and the lead author of the 2018 experiments and the pre-2011 band theorists left out.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B014 first, argues that the discovery is stable regardless of mechanism, that reproduction was unusually fast, and that there is no reason the case will improve by waiting.
responses.response: Your timing argument is fair, and I agree that unusually fast reproduction across many groups is real evidence of robustness. I do not agree that waiting costs nothing for B005 and something for B014, because for the clock the redefinition of the second is a use and not a validity condition, so the case is already complete today. For B014 the case may well be complete in a few years, and a longer record would also show which phases are intrinsic and which are sample dependent. On credit, your defence of Bistritzer as first author of a joint 2011 calculation is persuasive to me, and I withdraw my earlier suggestion to give the pair alone unless the committee finds the 2011 result is not joint. What still troubles me is that three seats force the experimental side onto the group leader while Cao, the lead author, and the earlier theorists remain outside, which you also acknowledge.

responses.point: Kroll supports B005 with Katori for the concept and first strontium lattice spectroscopy and Ye for record accuracy, and notes that priority among early proposals and parallel groups rests on memory and should be checked.
responses.response: I agree and I would add my own caveat to yours, since the two of us are leaning on recollection for the same point. The citation should say magic-wavelength trapping explicitly, so that it stays attached to the lattice clock and does not drift toward combs, ultrastable lasers or ion clocks. I am less comfortable than you with calling Katori the concept and Ye the performance without qualification, because Ye's group also made conceptual contributions on many-body effects, and a fair statement is that both made invention and realization steps with different emphasis. If the committee tests the early priority record and finds a third claimant, the attribution would need to be revisited, and I would rather say that openly now than treat the two-name list as settled.

responses.point: Danielsson asks whether Ye's share is co-invention or realization at record accuracy, and whether the committee should test that wording, while treating B005 as the safer choice on credit and B014 as the stronger new-phenomenon case.
responses.response: I think the honest answer is that it is both, and the citation I propose says so by crediting invention and realization jointly. The conceptual proposal and first strontium lattice work come from Tokyo, and Boulder took the same design to a regime of record accuracy and systematics that made the invention useful, including the many-body regime. I would not word it as Katori the inventor and Ye the engineer, because that understates the physics done in the realization. On your wider question, I share your instinct that the committee should care when nature surprises us, but I do not think that is the only prize criterion, and a mature measurement invention with a clean credit list is a legitimate choice this year.

uncertainties: Early priority among the Tokyo and Boulder lattice-clock proposals and first spectroscopy, and the strength of claims by other strontium, ytterbium and ultrastable-laser groups, rest on my memory and should be checked before the names are fixed.
Whether the committee accepts a third award in the neighbourhood of the 2005 and 2012 prizes, or prefers B014 as a new-phenomenon prize.
Whether eight years of work on moire graphene is enough maturity given unresolved mechanism and sample variability, which matters if the committee turns to B014.
If B014 is chosen, whether Bistritzer belongs beside MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, and how Cao and the earlier theorists should be treated in the discussion of credit.
statement.conflict_note: I direct WACQT and work in superconducting circuits and quantum computing, so B046 and, less directly, B024 and B015 are close to my own field. B046 is not in my preferred configuration and I would step back from deciding on it. B024 is only a listed alternative, and I would also step back if it were advanced. Chalmers colleagues Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson and co-author Anton Frisk Kockum are not credited on any shortlisted ballot. No personal or institutional connection to Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero or Bistritzer is apparent from my profile. I did not change my preferred configuration from round 1.
